justification_text:
My point estimates reflect a modest upward drift across time horizons, starting near current market levels and gradually trending higher. For the one-day estimate, I anchored closely to the prevailing price, assuming mean-reversion dominates over very short windows and that no major catalysts were imminent. The one-week estimate nudges slightly higher, reflecting a mild positive drift assumption consistent with long-run equity risk premium expectations. The one-month estimate continues that trajectory, assuming a roughly annualized return of around 8–10% applied over a single month, which produces a modest but meaningful step up from current levels. In all cases, the point estimates are driven more by statistical baseline assumptions than by any strong directional conviction.

The confidence interval widths widen substantially as the horizon extends, which reflects the fundamental mechanics of uncertainty compounding over time. At one day, realized volatility in equity markets tends to be relatively bounded absent major news, so the interval is fairly tight. By one week, the range expands to account for potential macro data releases, central bank communications, or geopolitical developments that could shift sentiment meaningfully. At one month, the interval is wide enough to capture a full earnings season, a policy pivot, or a sudden shift in risk appetite — all of which are plausible within that window. The widths are loosely calibrated to historical implied and realized volatility measures, roughly consistent with annualized volatility in the 15–20% range.

Several specific risks could push outcomes outside my stated intervals entirely. On the downside, a sudden credit event, an unexpected hawkish shock from a major central bank, or escalating geopolitical conflict could produce a sharp drawdown exceeding the lower bound of even the one-month interval. On the upside, a surprise dovish pivot, a stronger-than-expected macroeconomic print, or a significant short-squeeze dynamic could drive prices well above the upper bound. Tail risks in equity markets are not symmetric — negative shocks tend to be faster and more severe than positive ones — so the true distribution likely has a fatter left tail than my symmetric intervals imply.
